S24.supports: Iran expressed general willingness to resume talks through Pakistani mediation; an Iranian presidential-office official said Munir's visit produced valuable diplomatic achievements; a Pakistani government source said Pakistan told Tehran the U.S. would reverse the new sanctions before or during renewed talks. Reuters notes there was no immediate White House or State Department confirmation of that sanctions-reversal message.
S24.quality: HIGH; U.S.-sanctions reversal element is PAKISTANI-SOURCE CLAIM

S25.supports: Iran and Oman announced progress toward an interim Hormuz framework: a temporary joint navigation corridor, joint mine-clearing, continued technical negotiations on a permanent corridor and future administration, traffic management, navigational/security services, consultation with Gulf littoral states, and adherence to international law.

S26.supports: Trump said all mines had been detonated or removed from international waters of the Strait of Hormuz and warned that vessels laying new mines would be destroyed. Reuters separately reported Hormuz oil transits remained far below pre-war levels.
S26.quality: HIGH for FACT OF U.S. PRESIDENTIAL CLAIM; mine-clearance completeness remains a U.S. claim unless independently verified

S27.supports: Pakistan said its Tehran mission made significant progress on preventing escalation, reopening Hormuz, ending the conflict and reaching a negotiated settlement after Munir had spoken with Trump.

S28.supports: Growing gasoline queues in Tehran and discussion of reducing heavy fuel subsidies show economic pressure reaching household consumption; AP also reports continuing official defiance and no broad protest wave at publication.
S28.quality: HIGH; household/queue observations do not by themselves prove political capitulation or imminent unrest

S29.supports: Brent settled at $88.58 and WTI at $82.36, both down more than 3%, as traders treated sanctions and diplomatic movement as less threatening to physical supply than renewed major conflict.
S29.quality: HIGH; market pricing is a risk signal, not proof of Iranian intent or capability

S30.supports: The U.S. began returning diplomatic staff to Middle East missions and scaling back some emergency measures after Iran-war evacuations, indicating a lower assessed immediate escalation risk while not eliminating the possibility of renewed conflict.
S30.quality: HIGH; posture signal, not proof that Iran has abandoned kinetic options

S31.supports: The expanded U.S. sanctions campaign reaches counterparties and sectors including shipping, aviation, technology, gold and digital assets, while nearly 60 Iran-linked persons, entities and vessels were newly targeted.

S32.supports: Iranian officials described a temporary Hormuz routing proposal under which inbound Gulf traffic would pass through Iranian territorial waters while Iran and Oman continue 30-60 days of negotiations toward a permanent route and administration.
S32.quality: HIGH; shows a meaningful temporary Iranian operational role without establishing unilateral permanent authority

status_overrides.Hormuz leverage: STILL POWERFUL / JOINT CORRIDOR PATH NOW CONCRETE

three_angle_status.assessment: Tehran is trying to preserve the story that Washington must back down first. But Iran is already validating Pakistan's mediation and accepting a joint Oman implementation process before the old U.S. concessions have been restored.
three_angle_status.why: Relative to Iran's own prior stated terms, this is a retreat: the old MOU is not controlling, unilateral Hormuz authority has not been recognized, and Tehran is working through a new reciprocal framework under pressure. That is capitulation relative to its preferred negotiating position, even if it is packaged domestically as reciprocity or 'negotiating from strength.' It is not unconditional national surrender.

three_angle_status.assessment: Iran can still endure, but the cost of doing so is rising while the hoped-for economic insulation from partners is not visibly improving.
three_angle_status.why: Fuel queues and subsidy pressure are becoming visible at household level, U.S. sanctions are broadening toward counterparties, and earlier evidence already showed Chinese commercial de-risking and UAE financial/trade rupture. Survival remains possible; bargaining room is narrowing.

three_angle_status.assessment: Iran retains the ability to threaten or impose costs, but current observable indicators do not show that this option is becoming more effective or more credible.
three_angle_status.why: Threat rhetoric remains high, yet no public preparation surge has appeared; oil prices fell sharply rather than adding a larger Iran-war premium, and Washington is reducing some regional embassy emergency measures. That does not prove Iran cannot strike. It does show that current threats are not producing stronger external fear or visible U.S. defensive reaction.

paragraph5_update.title: Aug. 25 behavioral confirmation — what Iran accepted with Oman
paragraph5_update.text: Iran and Oman are now discussing a temporary joint corridor, joint mine-clearing, a permanent corridor, future administration, traffic management and maritime/security services, with consultations involving other Gulf littoral states and reference to international law. Iranian officials also describe a temporary routing design that preserves a meaningful Iranian operational role for inbound traffic. That is behaviorally consistent with Paragraph 5's shared/future-governance structure. It does not validate the later claim that Paragraph 5 had already granted Iran unilateral permanent control or a compulsory transit-toll right.

mou_now.text: The June MOU remains expired and non-controlling. What changed on Aug. 25 is that Iran and Oman moved from discussing a possible successor mechanism to a concrete phased maritime framework. The emerging structure reuses recognizable Paragraph 5 concepts — joint navigation, mine-clearing, future administration, services, littoral-state consultation and international law — while also preserving a meaningful temporary Iranian operational role. It is still a new post-collapse negotiation, not restoration of the old bargain. Tehran's political task is increasingly to describe a retreat from its preferred terms as proof that it did not capitulate. Relative to its prior demand that Washington reverse course first and restore the old MOU, however, Iran is already negotiating and accepting a shared implementation process before those benefits have returned. That is substantive capitulation from its prior bargaining position, not unconditional surrender of the Iranian state.

node_evidence.claim: Iran publicly says coercion should stop while mediated reporting says Tehran is willing to resume talks if sequencing produces a visible U.S. move.
node_evidence.confidence: High on statements; medium on unconfirmed U.S. sanctions-reversal message
node_evidence.editorial_note: Keep the Pakistani-source account of U.S. sanctions reversal separate from confirmed U.S. policy.

node_evidence.claim: Iran validated Pakistan's mediation and then accepted a phased Oman maritime framework.
node_evidence.editorial_note: This is stronger than rhetoric because both mediator and Iranian/Omani behavior moved.

node_evidence.claim: Iran is trying to preserve a narrative of negotiating from strength while its behavior shows a retreat from its prior preferred terms into a new post-collapse mechanism.
node_evidence.editorial_note: Call this capitulation relative to Iran's prior bargaining position, not unconditional surrender. Narrative purpose remains an inference; the changed terms and negotiating behavior are observable.

node_evidence.claim: Iran and Oman moved the joint-corridor path from hypothetical to a concrete phased framework.
node_evidence.editorial_note: The framework is not yet a final permanent navigation agreement.

node_evidence.claim: Trump says U.S. forces cleared all mines from international waters of Hormuz and will destroy new minelayers.
node_evidence.confidence: High for fact of statement; independent completeness verification not established
node_evidence.editorial_note: Do not convert the presidential claim into independently verified total demining.

node_evidence.claim: If the international lane is substantially clear, Iran's leverage increasingly comes from its ability to impose risk and contest rules rather than exclusive possession of a mine-clearing solution.
node_evidence.editorial_note: Conditional on the practical extent of U.S. mine clearance; shipping remains heavily depressed.

node_evidence.claim: The Aug. 25 Oman-Iran framework again describes joint/future administration, littoral-state consultation and international law rather than recognition of unilateral permanent Iranian transit authority.
node_evidence.editorial_note: Iran retains a meaningful temporary operational role; that is not the same as recognition of exclusive permanent authority.

node_evidence.claim: Iran's public line says U.S. coercion must stop and Washington must change course.
Iranian officials simultaneously keep coercive retaliation against U.S. interests and energy chokepoints on the table.
node_evidence.editorial_note: Threat language is not evidence of an operational decision to strike.

node_evidence.claim: Iran's observable diplomatic behavior is engagement: Pakistan mediation was publicly validated and Oman produced a concrete maritime framework.
node_evidence.editorial_note: Behavior does not prove a final settlement has been accepted.

node_evidence.claim: The clearest current distinction is defiant public framing versus practical retreat into mediated negotiation and shared implementation.
node_evidence.editorial_note: Plain language: Iran is trying to show it did not capitulate, while the process itself shows concession from its previous terms.

node_evidence.claim: A Pakistani source says Washington's new sanctions could be reversed before or during renewed talks, giving Tehran a possible way to say Washington moved first.
node_evidence.editorial_note: Reuters reported no immediate White House or State Department confirmation; show this as a mediated claim, not an agreed U.S. commitment.

node_evidence.claim: Negotiating position is weakening relative to Iran's own prior terms.
node_evidence.editorial_note: Iran can win face-saving concessions while still having retreated from its previous demand that Washington restore the old bargain first.

node_evidence.claim: The wait-it-out position is weakening as household stress and counterparty sanctions exposure rise.
node_evidence.confidence: High on underlying facts; medium-high on strategic direction
node_evidence.editorial_note: Do not equate economic pain with automatic regime collapse. The narrower claim is reduced bargaining room.

node_evidence.claim: Kinetic coercion remains available, but current coercive credibility is not strengthening.
node_evidence.editorial_note: Falling oil risk premium and easing U.S. embassy precautions are external behavior signals, not proof that Iranian capability is gone.

node_evidence.claim: All three Iranian paths remain available, but none is improving Tehran's bargaining position: negotiation now requires retreat from prior terms, endurance is becoming costlier, and coercive threats are not generating stronger external fear.
node_evidence.editorial_note: Update if Washington grants major front-loaded relief, Iranian economic channels recover, or verified military preparation/coalition fragmentation changes the board.
